reader.title: Eldorado election violence of 1888
bases: About 100 armed white men guarded the roads into Eldorado on election day and shot, beat or drove back Black voters generally, killing one and bayoneting Jordan Gray, after a weekend of whippings across the county (A1, A2).

Two independent letters-based reports (A1 from Union County white men, A2 from a letter to the Republican committee) agree that armed men guarded the roads to Eldorado on election day and drove back, shot at and beat Black voters; the deaths and Jordan Gray's beating rest on A1 alone, and A4 gives a different count of the dead.

summary.text: The Eldorado election violence of 1888 was a series of attacks on Black voters by armed white men at Eldorado, the seat of Union County, Arkansas, on election day, Monday, September 3, 1888, and the nights before it.

According to Union County white men quoted from Little Rock, about 100 armed men guarded the roads into town, killed one Black man, and beat and bayoneted another, Jordan Gray, who was left confined to his bed.
Republican and Union Labor sources blamed Democrats and gave death counts ranging from one to sixteen.
Union County had no railroad or telegraph, and the accounts that reached outside papers came from residents who had left it.
In the week before the election, the office that printed the county's Union Labor newspaper was wrecked, an act the Little Rock dispatch attributed to Democrats.
On Saturday night, September 1, Democrats began whipping Black men who intended to vote for Norwood; the dispatch counted twenty-five flogged.
Press Neal, who lived eight miles north of El Dorado, was whipped for saying he would vote as he pleased, and Sandy Newton and Aaron Cobb were also whipped.
On Sunday the attackers went to a Black church, killed one man and wounded several others.
At six o'clock on election morning, 100 white men armed with guns and pistols assembled at Eldorado "to direct the election."
Before the polls opened they had killed one Black man and whipped another so severely that he was expected to die; neither was named.
Armed men guarded every road into town and drove back Black men coming in, and those who did not "strike a trot homeward" were shot or whipped, one resident said.
Jordan Gray was made to take off his shirt and was then pounded with guns and prodded with bayonets; when the informant left, Gray was in bed.

The Republican committee's letter called the road guards "the militia" and said some Black men were shot at on a by-way, others beaten at home, and some in El Dorado forced to vote the "Bourbon ticket."
After the voting, white witnesses who opposed the attacks were made at gunpoint to promise not to prosecute.
Elsewhere in the county, a Black man was reported killed at Lisbon, and at Champagnolle masked men destroyed the ballot box; that night the store of Cook, a Norwood supporter, burned.
No report of an inquest, arrest or trial for the Eldorado killings or beatings appears in the coverage.
The New-York Tribune broke the story on September 13 in a St. Louis special headed "A Vote or a Life in Arkansas," with the deck "Premeditated Murder of Negroes at the Polls."
Its follow-up on September 17, "Political Outrages in Arkansas," called the events outrages "without parallel in the political history of the State."

On September 20 the Indianapolis Journal printed, as "Bloody Fraud in Arkansas," a letter from Union Labor leader R. B. Carl Lee accusing Governor Hughes of arming the Democratic clubs with state Winchesters.
The Portland Daily Press had summarized that letter a day earlier, and the Journal reprinted it on October 23 under "Seven Whites Killed."

A New York Mail and Express account ran in the Vermont Phoenix on September 21 and the Burlington Weekly Free Press on September 28, the latter headed "A Reign of Terror Again Inaugurated among the Blacks."
These northern accounts rested on Union Labor or Republican informants or unnamed white residents, and only the first Tribune report named Jordan Gray.

Arkansas papers in the coverage did not describe the attacks: the Forrest City Times noted only that E. T. Cook's store at Champagnolle had burned, and the Russellville Democrat dismissed complaints of "alleged democratic outrages" elsewhere.

The Little Rock dispatch reported one Black man killed at Eldorado and an unconfirmed sixteen dead countywide, while Carl Lee wrote that seven white Union Labor men were killed and over twenty wounded; the committee letter reported no deaths.

The armed men were "100 white men" in the dispatch, "the militia" in the committee letter, and state-armed Democratic clubs in Carl Lee's letter, which also placed the whippings on Sunday night rather than Saturday.

accounts.label: Little Rock dispatch from Union County white citizens
accounts.gist: 100 armed white men at Eldorado killed one Black man and whipped another nearly to death; roads guarded; Jordan Gray beaten and bayoneted; sixteen reported dead.

accounts.label: Letter to the Republican State Central Committee
accounts.gist: Saturday-night whippings; militia guarded all roads to El Dorado, drove Black men home, shot at and beat some; no deaths reported.

accounts.label: Union Labor leader R. B. Carl Lee
accounts.gist: Democratic clubs armed with state rifles whipped over twenty Black men Sunday night and on Monday killed seven white Union Labor men; Eldorado poll books burned.

accounts.label: Globe-Democrat correspondent via Mail and Express
accounts.gist: Union Labor office wrecked, Black men stripped and whipped, a church attack killed one; Champagnolle ballot box destroyed and Cook's store burned.

framing.detail: New-York Tribune: 'A Vote or a Life in Arkansas' and 'Premeditated Murder of Negroes at the Polls.'
New-York Tribune: 'Political Outrages in Arkansas,' outrages 'without parallel in the political history of the State.'
Indianapolis Journal: 'Bloody Fraud in Arkansas,' a story of murder and fraud 'almost incredible.'
Vermont papers reprint the Mail and Express under 'How Arkansas Was Carried' and 'A Reign of Terror Again Inaugurated among the Blacks.'
Russellville Democrat dismisses 'alleged democratic outrages' and points to 'republican outrages' instead.
Forrest City Times notes Cook's store fire as routine state news.

versions.value: One Black man killed at Eldorado before the polls opened
Sixteen killed since Sunday evening (reported second-hand)
Seven white Union Labor men killed, over twenty wounded
No deaths reported at El Dorado

conflicts.note: All sources are partisan or second-hand; none is local or sworn.

versions.value: Democratic clubs armed with State Winchesters by the governor

conflicts.note: Versions may describe the same body; A5 says the county's militia was organized after the campaign opened.

record_check.dossier: Jordan Gray was beaten and bayoneted and reported in bed, not killed; the one Black man killed at Eldorado is unnamed. Others whipped before the election: Press Neal, Sandy Newton, Aaron Cobb.
Black (the attacks targeted 'negroes' coming to vote; Gray is described among them); A4 alone claims white Union Labor men were killed.
One unnamed Black man at Eldorado per A1 (plus church and Lisbon killings elsewhere in the county); seven white men per A4; sixteen rumored. Gray is not among the dead.

record_check.record: killed Black people ... Jordan Gray was stripped and bayoneted
record_check.dossier: One Black man killed at Eldorado, another whipped near death; Gray stripped, beaten with guns and prodded with bayonets, survived to be 'in bed'.
Democrats: 100 armed white men (A1), 'the militia' (A2), or Democratic clubs armed with state rifles (A4).

At least five white papers carried accounts (New-York Tribune, Indianapolis Journal, Portland Daily Press, Vermont Phoenix, Burlington Weekly Free Press), plus two Arkansas papers touching related matters.

info: Monday, September 3, 1888 (election day), with whippings from Saturday night, September 1, and a church attack Sunday
